sentences.text: There's something terrifying about the way this beautiful face is looking at you.
This is The Fallen Angel, painted by Alexandre Cabanel in 1847.
And this is no monster with claws.
It's an angel with wings.
Young, flawless, almost holy.
But look at his face.
He's weeping.
There's one tear caught at the edge of his eye.
And yet it doesn't look like grief at all.
Look into his eyes.
There's rage in there.
A quiet, patient, sleepless rage.
As if something in him has just gone cold forever.
According to the old story of the fall, God cast this angel out of heaven, and he became the Devil.
And Cabanel seems to capture something few painters dared.
Not the fall itself, but the first minute after it.
The moment when an angel understands the door is shut for good.
Imagine being thrown out of the only home you ever had.
Would you ask to come back?
Would you bow your head and wait?
Or would you swear to make them pay?
That's what makes this painting so hard to look at.
The angel is still beautiful, but his eyes no longer look kind.
The tear says one thing, the stare says another.
And perhaps that's the most frightening part.
Maybe evil never arrives looking like evil.
Maybe it begins with a wound, then becomes a grudge, and eventually turns into rage.
So look at him one more time.
Do you see an angel crying for what he lost?
Or the first second of the Devil?

sources.claim: It was painted in 1847, when the artist was 24 years old, and depicts the Devil after his fall from Heaven.
Depicting an angel expelled from heaven by God, the painting shows an enraged Lucifer, with his hands crossed and tears running from his eyes.
Lucifer glares out angrily from behind his arm, tears visible in his eyes.
Depicting an angel expelled from heaven by God, the painting shows an enraged Lucifer, with his hands crossed and tears running from his eyes.
Cabanel opted for a subject not often represented in French painting: the fall from Heaven of the Fallen Angel, who went on to become the Devil.
